title: DLLs and PLL Applications
intro: Delay-locked loops, and the jobs that make PLLs worth more than a piece of wire: frequency multiplication and synthesis, skew removal and jitter cleanup (Razavi, Sections 16.4 and 16.5).

blocks.text: To make four clock phases exactly 1 ns apart you could lock a two-stage differential ring to 250 MHz. Alternatively, send the clock through four voltage-controlled delay stages and servo their delay until the last tap lines up with the input: the line then delays by exactly one period and each tap is $T_{in}/4$ later than the previous one.

blocks.alt: Clock input passes through four delay cells in a row with taps CK1 to CK4. A PD/CP/LPF block compares the input clock with CK4 and drives a control line common to all four cells.
blocks.caption: A delay-locked loop.

items: Less noise than a PLL: a corrupted edge leaves the end of a delay line, whereas an oscillator recirculates it.
Easier dynamics: the delay line changes its delay at once, $\Phi_{out}/V_{cont} = K_{VCDL}$ with no integrator, so the loop has the order of its filter.
Close to all-pass for input phase: slow input wander is tracked, fast wander passes straight through the line, so the gain is near one at both ends, with a possible dip or peak in between.

False lock: if the line's delay range spans more than one period, it may lock at $2T_{in}$ instead of $T_{in}$; extra circuitry prevents this. Stage and load mismatch spread the tap spacing, so devices must be large and laid out carefully.

blocks.text: Just as an amplifier gains $M$ by feeding back $1/M$ of its output, a PLL multiplies frequency by feeding back $f_{out}/M$ through a counter. In lock $f_{out}/M = f_{in}$:

blocks.tex: f_{out} = M f_{in}, \qquad H(s) \to M \text{ as } s \to 0

blocks.text: Unlike the voltage amplifier, the multiplication is exact. The VCO plus divider act as one VCO of gain $K_{VCO}/M$ and intercept $\omega_0/M$, which is why $M$ appears in $\omega_n$ and $\zeta$.

Make $M$ programmable from a channel-select word and the output steps in increments of $f_{REF}$, with the relative accuracy of the reference (usually a crystal oscillator). This is how radios generate carriers with ppm accuracy and fine channel spacing. Noise, spurs, settling, range and power are the ongoing design challenges.

A clock entering a large chip passes a big buffer before it is distributed, and arrives late relative to data. Put the buffer inside a PLL (or DLL) loop and compare the buffered clock with the input: the infinite loop gain divides the buffer delay down to zero, just as a voltage offset inside a high-gain loop is suppressed ($V_{out} = (AV_{in} + V_M)/(1 + A) \to V_{in}$). The VCO output itself is not aligned, but it is not used. Without the need to multiply, a DLL is preferred because it is quieter.

Because the closed loop is low-pass for input phase, a PLL with a 10 MHz bandwidth on a 1 GHz input acts as a 20 MHz-wide band-pass filter around 1 GHz for jitter. Data corrupted by crosstalk, package parasitics and noise is retimed by a flip-flop clocked by a clean clock; when no separate clock is sent (an optical link, say), a clock-recovery PLL with a narrow bandwidth extracts it from the data itself.

blocks.title: Frequency synthesis
blocks.text: $f_{ref} = 10\text{ MHz}$ and $N = 240$. Find $f_{out}$. What $N$ gives 2.45 GHz?

blocks.title: Channel plan
blocks.text: A synthesizer must cover 2.400 to 2.480 GHz in 1 MHz steps. Choose $f_{REF}$ and the range of $M$. What limits the loop bandwidth?
solution: The loop bandwidth must stay well below 1 MHz (about 100 kHz) for stability and spur suppression, which also makes settling slow: the price of fine steps with an integer divider.

blocks.title: DLL tap spacing
blocks.text: An eight-stage DLL runs at 500 MHz. What is the tap spacing, and what happens if it falsely locks to two periods?
solution: Locked to $2T_{in}$: 500 ps spacing, so taps $k$ and $k+4$ coincide and the phases are useless as eight distinct phases.
blocks.answer: 250 ps; false lock doubles it to 500 ps.

blocks.title: Keeping dynamics with a divider
blocks.text: A loop was designed with $M = 1$. A divider of $M = 100$ is added. If nothing else changes, how do $\omega_n$ and $\zeta$ change, and what pump current restores them?
solution: Both scale as $\sqrt{K_{VCO}/M}$, so each falls by $\sqrt{100} = 10$.
Raising $I_P$ by 100 restores both, since they scale as $\sqrt{I_PK_{VCO}/M}$.
